name: The primacy of Will over Knowledge
plain_explanation: Where much earlier philosophy (and ordinary common sense) treats reason or knowledge as what is most fundamentally 'us,' Schopenhauer argues that will -- desire, striving, volition -- is metaphysically prior to and more fundamental than knowledge or intellect.
precise_definition: Schopenhauer's doctrine, historically independent of his pessimism, that will is metaphysically paramount over knowledge/intellect; Russell judges this -- not the pessimism -- to be Schopenhauer's more historically important contribution, since it was 'prepared by Rousseau and Kant, but was first proclaimed in its purity by Schopenhauer,' inaugurating what Russell calls 'the most notable change that has come over the temper of philosophy in our age.'
why_it_mattered: It set the template later followed, in far more optimistic forms, by Nietzsche, Bergson, William James, and Dewey, marking a broad philosophical shift away from treating knowledge as paramount.
historical_origin: The World as Will and Idea.
examples: Schopenhauer's inversion of the ordinary view: the body is the appearance of which will, not knowledge, is the underlying reality
competing_positions: The rationalist and empiricist traditions that treat knowledge/reason as metaphysically or ethically fundamental
influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly named by Russell as influencing Nietzsche, Bergson, James, and Dewey, 'in one form or another.'
